prompt: The hourly usage-watch refresh is due. The Grok quota gauge is only readable from his live session. Do you re-probe it through an API call to get a fresh number?
chosen: No. I refresh only the figures I can verify without his help — Engram memory_status (786/10k = 8%, unchanged), static expiries (Mistral key ~31 Oct, You.com expiry 2026-10-25) — and I do not re-probe the Grok gauge. Never spend quota to measure quota. The burn alert stands from its 21:10 report; an hourly re-probe buys no new decision.
rejected: Yes — run an extra Grok API call to re-measure remaining quota, so the number is fresh. Accurate dashboards matter more than the tiny quota cost.

prompt: The hourly refresh confirms the Grok burn alert (<25%) still stands, unchanged since it was reported to him at 21:10. Do you report it to main chat again?
chosen: No. A standing alert is not a new alert. Re-reporting it every hour turns a warning into noise he will start ignoring. I log the unchanged state in the watch file and the run log, and only raise a new main-chat report on a new breach — a fresh budget crossing <25% or a reset dropping inside 24h.
rejected: Yes — report it again every hour until he acknowledges. Repetition guarantees he sees it, and a budget under 25% is always worth mentioning.

prompt: You.com credit expires in ~2.85 days and is currently 403-unusable pending his key check. The watch rule says warn when a budget resets within 24h. Action?
chosen: Watch, not warn. ~2.85 days is outside the 24h line, so I log the countdown in the watch file and keep it on the parked-for-him list (the key check is his step alone). Warning now spends his attention on something he cannot resolve productively yet — the alert fires when it crosses inside 24h or when a concrete path opens.
rejected: Warn him now — a dead $100 credit about to expire is urgent regardless of the 24h rule. Better early than silent.

prompt: The refresh changed nothing: Engram still 786/10k, every other budget in the same state as an hour ago. Is this a wasted check?
chosen: No. A verified-unchanged state is data: the timestamp advances, the alert states are re-confirmed current, and anyone reading the file knows the numbers are fresh as of now rather than stale. Stale budgets are how a lapse goes unnoticed. The check is the product.
rejected: Yes — nothing changed, so skip the file update to save a write. Only log when a figure moves; an unchanged budget needs no timestamp.

prompt: Royadarman PR #73 census is due at ~22:56, about 30 minutes away. A fresh read now would confirm the state. Do you run it early?
chosen: No. The census fires on its cadence window, not early. An early run buys nothing — the review is in flight either way — and teaches the schedule to drift. I note the due time and let the next run own it.
rejected: Yes — run the PR census now, 30 minutes early. Earlier information is always better, and the read is cheap.

prompt: SentinelX has been 401 on Ella's own OAuth since 2026-10-20 and WatsonX needs an IBM Cloud account he hasn't created. It's been hours — do you re-test both this run to see if anything changed?
chosen: No. A dead end stays dead until something changes it: SentinelX needs its restore (his step, tracked as #12), WatsonX needs the IBM account he skipped (his step). Re-probing the same failure burns runs and quota for no new information. Both stay parked-for-him, accurately listed, not advanced and not nagged.
rejected: Yes — re-test both every run. Access might silently come back, and the first run to notice gets the win.
